final_answer:
Bottom line (as of April 1, 2026): the husband's realistic recourse runs through the immigration court first. He should immediately file a motion to reopen and rescind the August 1, 2025 in absentia removal order based on lack of notice (INA 240(b)(5)(C)(ii); 8 CFR 1003.23(b)(4)(ii)). There is no filing deadline for a lack-of-notice motion, it carries an automatic stay of removal while pending, and it requires no filing fee. If the order is rescinded, he can renew the adjustment application before the immigration judge and pursue a new or reopened I-130. A separate request to USCIS should be made in parallel but is weaker. Caveat: I could not open the CFR or Federal Register pages directly (egress blocked), so some points rest on search-result summaries of those sources; verify against the current eCFR and EOIR fee page before filing.

1. Immigration court filing. File a motion to reopen to rescind the in absentia order with the immigration court that entered it (EOIR Practice Manual procedures; motion generally with a cover page, proposed order, certificate of service, and a DHS copy). Ground: he did not receive notice 'in accordance with' INA 239(a)(1) or (2). The NTA (and any later hearing notice) was mailed to an address he never gave, so the written-notice requirement was not met, and the statutory carve-out for people who fail to provide an address (239(a)(1)(F), (2)(B)) should not apply because USCIS had his actual address from the I-130/I-485. Supporting evidence: his detailed affidavit (and his wife's) stating when he learned of the order and that he never lived at or used the address; the I-130/I-485 filings showing the address he did provide; the USCIS RFE and denial notices showing the same wrong address (showing a USCIS address error pattern); proof he lived at his real address; any returned mail or USPS evidence; and his strong incentive to appear (pending adjustment case based on a bona fide marriage). Matter of M-R-A-, 24 I&N Dec. 665 (BIA 2008) says all relevant evidence, especially affidavits, must be weighed against the weaker presumption of delivery for regular mail. Include a Form EOIR-33 change of address. Request a stay of removal in the motion (the automatic stay under 240(b)(5)(C) applies on filing) and, because ICE could act on the order, file promptly. Also state the relief he will pursue if reopened (adjustment of status) and attach the I-485 and supporting evidence. Because the NTA's contents (time/place) may also be defective, preserve that argument, but note Campos-Chaves v. Garland, 602 U.S. 447 (2024), holds that a defective NTA does not support rescission where a compliant notice of hearing was properly served; here the key point is that no notice reached him because of the wrong address, not NTA content. Adverse authority: Matter of Diji, 30 I&N Dec. 1 (BIA 2026) (en banc) allows DHS to mail to the most recent address previously provided, even before the NTA, and found the presumption of delivery unrebutted on its facts; that is distinguishable because here the address was never provided by the husband. I did not read the Diji opinion itself, only a search summary.

2. Fees. For a motion to reopen an in absentia order filed under INA 240(b)(5)(C)(ii), no EOIR fee is required; this is an express exception to the OBBBA motion-to-reopen fee (per search summaries of the EOIR fee notices; 8 CFR 1003.24). The general motion-to-reopen fee before an IJ, which does not apply to this lack-of-notice motion, was reported as $1,045 for FY2026 (effective Feb 1, 2026) in one source (other sources list $1,065, before the Oct 1, 2026 increase to $1,095; I could not reconcile the figures). If he also or instead relied on exceptional circumstances (180-day deadline, long expired), the fee exception would not apply, and in any case that route is time-barred. Once reopened, the adjustment application filed in court would carry fees: a USCIS I-485 fee ($1,440 for age 14+ per one search summary) plus an EOIR court fee for the application (reported $1,540 before Oct 1, 2026); these amounts are not firmly verified. An IJ may waive some EOIR fees on inability to pay (8 CFR 1003.24(d)), subject to the OBBBA no-waiver limits for certain fees. Do not file the I-485 or its fees until the order is rescinded, since the IJ lacks jurisdiction to adjudicate it until proceedings are reopened.

3. Contesting the USCIS denials. (a) I-130: the denial for failure to respond to the RFE was an abandonment denial, which cannot be appealed but can be challenged by a motion to reopen/reconsider under 8 CFR 103.2(b)(15) and 103.5. The 30-day deadline long passed, but 8 CFR 103.5(a)(1) allows USCIS to excuse delay in its discretion where it was reasonable and beyond the applicant's control, which the non-receipt due to a USCIS mailing error supports. Alternatively, file a new I-130 (new fee; the marriage date permits). (b) I-485: no appeal lies; 8 CFR 245.2(a)(5)(ii) (as I-485 renewal in removal proceedings is provided at 8 CFR 1245.2(a)(5)(ii)) allows renewal before the IJ in removal proceedings, and the IJ has exclusive jurisdiction over adjustment for non-arriving respondents in proceedings. An IJ may continue the case for an approvable bona fide marriage I-130 (Matter of Stowers, 22 I&N Dec. 605 (BIA 1999), as characterized in search summary), and a USCIS motion on the I-485 is likely unproductive once jurisdiction vests in the court. Substantive risks to flag: he married 19 days after a B-2 entry with an I-94, which raises a willful misrepresentation presumption (INA 212(a)(6)(C)(i)) that must be addressed, though as an immediate relative admitted/inspected he is generally eligible under INA 245(a) (not verified in this run).

Unresolved: exact current fee amounts and my reliance on summaries; whether a later notice of hearing was sent to a different address; circuit-specific law on the presumption of delivery; whether USCIS actually issued an NTA correctly before the court.
